characterized_levers.name: Technical Feasibility Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy. Immediate: Demonstrators built → Systemic: 15% increased policy traction due to concrete evidence → Strategic: Enhanced credibility in procurement negotiations.
options: Focus demonstrator efforts on a single, highly secure authentication method, such as FIDO2, on a mainstream Android device.
Develop demonstrators for both FIDO2 on GrapheneOS and a browser-based fallback, accepting slightly longer development timelines.
Explore passwordless authentication via blockchain-anchored identity and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) alongside FIDO2 and browser-based fallback demonstrators.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Technical Risk vs. Scope. Weakness: The options don't explicitly address the cost implications of each demonstrator approach.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on demonstrating technical feasibility to impact policy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of the technical demonstrators on policy traction, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to demonstrator development.
characterized_levers.description: The Technical Feasibility Strategy translates resilience goals into concrete, testable artifacts by guiding the scope and methods of demonstrators. It chooses authentication approaches to pursue (FIDO2/WebAuthn on Android/GrapheneOS, browser-based fallback, hardware tokens) and defines success metrics (number and quality of demonstrators, interoperability with OpenID Connect, alignment with NSIS/eIDAS). It assesses risk, budget, and timelines to ensure credible evidence for platform-neutral paths. This lever informs policy, procurement, and standards work by providing empirical input for decision-making. It also identifies critical dependency signals and gaps that could become blockers.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Strong synergy with Policy Advocacy Strategy and EU Standards Engagement Strategy: demonstrator results provide credible, data-driven input for policy proposals and EU-aligned standards work, while informing coalition messaging and stakeholder discussions. It also supports Procurement Influence Strategy by transforming technical feasibility into procurement criteria that vendors can meet.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Primary conflicts arise from time and cost trade-offs: pursuing ambitious demonstrators may strain budget and schedule, delaying procurement work and policy messaging. Concentrating on deeper, security-heavy demos can crowd out alternative approaches and limit market tests. Potential clashes with Procurement Influence Strategy when timelines drive language constraints.

characterized_levers.name: Policy Advocacy Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Policy advocacy shapes procurement. Immediate: Policy proposals submitted → Systemic: 20% greater likelihood of influencing AltID requirements → Strategic: Increased adoption of platform-neutral standards.
options: Focus advocacy on continuity of service and supplier concentration risks, avoiding direct privacy arguments.
Balance continuity arguments with privacy and democratic accountability concerns, broadening the coalition.
Prioritize open-source governance and community-led development models for digital identity, framing platform neutrality as a public good.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Political Risk vs. Coalition Size. Weakness: The options don't consider the potential for regulatory capture by incumbent vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on policy advocacy shaping procurement, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of policy advocacy on influencing AltID requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to advocacy focus.
characterized_levers.description: The Policy Advocacy Strategy shapes how resilience, continuity, and supplier-concentration risks are framed for policymakers, procurement authorities, and the public. It produces formal policy proposals and stakeholder communications to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, casting platform-neutral approaches as risk-mitigation and public-good reform. It coordinates messaging across coalitions, tracks decision gates, and links technical feasibility results to regulatory reform. Key metrics include published proposals, formal responses from authorities, and the inclusion of platform-neutral language in procurement and policy documents. It also monitors for regulatory capture risks and ensures privacy and democratic accountability remain central.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Strong synergy with Coalition Building Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy: policy proposals gain legitimacy through broad coalitions and translate into concrete procurement language, increasing the likelihood of platform-neutral terms being adopted. It also informs EU Standards alignment by elevating privacy accountability as a governance priority.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Risks include potential regulatory capture by incumbents and political fragility of messaging. Narrow framing may alienate privacy or civil-society advocates, and domestic policy goals could diverge from EU directions, complicating Coalition Building and EU Standards work. This tension can constrain Procurement Influence Strategy if policy reminders tighten language too rigidly.

characterized_levers.name: Coalition Building Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Coalition strength amplifies advocacy. Immediate: Stakeholder engagement increased → Systemic: 30% stronger advocacy position in procurement discussions → Strategic: Greater political pressure for platform neutrality.
options: Build a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders.
Expand the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.
Actively recruit dissenting voices from within the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to foster internal debate.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Speed vs. Breadth of Support. Weakness: The options fail to address the potential for conflicting priorities within the coalition.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on coalition building to amplify advocacy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of coalition strength on advocacy position, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to coalition composition.
characterized_levers.description: The Coalition Building Strategy expands the network of supporters for platform neutrality, combining civil society, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security professionals, and contingency-planning stakeholders. It amplifies policy and procurement efforts by increasing legitimacy, multiplying channels to decision-makers, and surfacing risk scenarios. The strategy curates engagement plans, facilitates dialogues between public authorities and non-governmental actors, and helps surface counterarguments and trade-offs. Metrics include breadth of coalition, frequency of engagements, and measured impact on advocacy strength in procurement discussions. It also anticipates internal conflicts and creates mechanisms for rapid alignment when priorities shift.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Synergy with Policy Advocacy Strategy and EU Standards Engagement Strategy: a broad, credible coalition amplifies policy proposals and helps embed Danish positions into EU discussions, raising the political cost for blocking platform-neutral approaches. It also improves responsiveness to procurement feedback by presenting unified stakeholder positions.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Risks include decision paralysis and internal conflicts among diverse actors with conflicting priorities. Broad coalitions may slow consensus and dilute messages, creating friction with Policy Advocacy and EU Standards engagements when positions collide. It can also hinder agile decision-making necessary for procurement milestones.

characterized_levers.name: Procurement Influence Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Procurement influence drives adoption. Immediate: Platform-neutral language included in procurement documents → Systemic: 25% faster scaling through mandated supplier diversity → Strategic: Reduced long-term dependency on Apple and Google.
options: Focus on including general language about supplier concentration risk in AltID procurement documents.
Advocate for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths.
Propose a 'digital sovereignty bonus' in procurement scoring, rewarding vendors who demonstrably reduce platform dependency.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Specificity vs. Implementability. Weakness: The options don't account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on procurement influence driving adoption, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of procurement influence on scaling, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to procurement language.
characterized_levers.description: The Procurement Influence Strategy works to embed platform-neutral and fallback requirements into procurement documents and vendor evaluations. It seeks language that constrains vendor lock-in, mandates certified fallback capabilities, and rewards suppliers who demonstrably reduce dependence on a single platform. It coordinates with policy and standards teams to craft procurement language and supports market-testing with supplier outreach. Success metrics include platform-neutral clauses in RFPs, improved bid diversity, and shorter procurement cycles through clearer criteria. It must anticipate gaming by vendors and preserve flexibility for evolving EU standards.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Synergy with Technical Feasibility Strategy and Coalition Building Strategy: demonstrable feasibility informs procurement language, while a broad coalition sustains vendor engagement and market testing, broadening accepted supplier options and reducing lock-in risk. This also aligns with EU standards engagements by harmonizing requirements across borders.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Conflicts include risk of gaming procurement rules by vendors and pushback from incumbents seeking to preserve control. Overly prescriptive terms may impede innovation or EU alignment, and national priorities can clash with broader market realities, limiting coalition leverage. This can alienate small suppliers and reduce agility in testing platform-neutral approaches.

characterized_levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: EU standards engagement creates broader impact. Immediate: Input provided to relevant EU bodies → Systemic: 10% increased alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements → Strategic: Enhanced interoperability and reduced lock-in across Europe.
options: Monitor relevant EU bodies and technical working groups, providing occasional input on interoperability.
Actively engage with EU bodies, advocating for platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms in eIDAS2 and related standards.
Champion a 'sovereign identity sandbox' within the EU Digital Identity Wallet framework to test and validate platform-neutral authentication models.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Resource Allocation vs. Scope of Influence. Weakness: The options don't address the potential for EU standards to be influenced by large platform vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on EU standards engagement creating broader impact, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of EU standards engagement on alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to EU engagement strategies.
characterized_levers.description: The EU Standards Engagement Strategy engages EU bodies, technical working groups, and interoperability fora to align Danish ambitions with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements. It channels demonstrations and policy asks into eIDAS2, NSIS, and interoperability efforts, seeking early alignment, shared standards, and portability assurances. It coordinates with national policy and procurement teams to reflect EU requirements in national plans, while guarding against platform-specific dependencies. Metrics include EU input delivered, alignment improvements, and inclusion of Danish positions in EU policy documents.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Synergy with Policy Advocacy Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy: EU-level alignment strengthens domestic policy proposals and procurement terms, ensuring Danish language reflects European norms while advancing platform-neutral and certified fallback goals. It also informs national coalitions about EU expectations, supporting broader legitimacy.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: EU-level influence can be constrained by political cycles, resource limits, and vendor lobbying. Domestic priorities may conflict with EU timelines, risking mismatch with national procurement cycles and potentially inviting regulatory friction if EU standards press for costly implementations. It may also clash with domestic sovereignty aims and coalition patience.
